content:
I noticed that the module system effectively treats @[inline] as @[expose] for definitions imported as meta, in the sense of not necessarily requiring a public meta import to use these definitions in public meta definitions downstream.

I think I see why; my question here is not whether that's expected, but what the criterion is that a metaprogrammer should check in order to determine if a given declaration's import needs to be public meta or just meta on the basis of this declaration appearing in a public meta definition. (I'm working on tooling to adjust imports.)

Example:

code

Module Foo:

module

-- set_option trace.Compiler.inferVisibility true -- see below
public def baz : Bool := true
@[inline] public def bazInlined : Bool := true

Separate module:

module

meta import Foo

meta def foo := baz
/--
error: Invalid public `meta` definition `bar`, `baz` is not accessible here; consider adding `public meta import Foo`
-/
#guard_msgs in
public meta def bar := foo

/-! But, if we use `bazInlined` tagged with `@[inline]`: -/

meta def fooWithInline := bazInlined
-- No error
public meta def barWithInline := fooWithInline

What follows is my attempt to figure out what I could check:

I see isTemplateLike which seems to govern this, and allows this on bases other than inlinability. E.g. replacing @[inline] with @[specialize] yields the same behavior.

Chasing references, this then seems to be referenced in shouldExportBody, and in turn in markDeclPublicRec, which modifies a (non-persistent) env extension inspectable via isDeclTransparent. (set_option trace.Compiler.inferVisibility true is informative here!) That environment extension affects what ends up in two extensions that seem to hold code, whose meanings I don't understand yet (baseExt and monoExt). In particular, the value of the Decl stored here is an .extern when not transparent.

So we have (in the downstream module) (← getBaseDecl? ``baz).map (·.value) matches some (.extern { entries := [.opaque] }), whereas (← getBaseDecl? ``bazInlined).map (·.value) matches some (.code _). So, if we need this declaration in a public meta position while its import was only meta imported, this approach would say "now check if you have .code anyway, and if so, this declaration can be in e.g. a public meta position without its import being public (only meta)."

But I'm really out of the area where I understand what invariants should hold about things like .code and .extern and whether I'm checking the right thing. :) Is there a better approach? This feels like quite a workaround.
Does it make sense to have that kind of complex logic in more places than just shake? I'd rather like not to
Yeah, I'm working on #find_home (figure out where you can move a declaration) and #min_imports, which used to exist (and be quite useful!) but have been broken since the module system arrived.

(Note, #min_imports is effectively "shake on a single file", and indeed is unnecessary if we could run shake on a single file. But we get it more or less for free if we have #find_home, which is the more important feature.)
You can always compute an overapproximation and then run shake :)

Indeed, I could probably conservatively insist on public meta import, but it does put me into a strange situation where the imports I claim are necessary are possibly not actually even provided yet by the imports in the actual file. :sweat_smile:

Interestingly, I think this exposes a bug in shake? :eyes: (Maybe you already know about it, I'm not sure!) Shake always suggests weakening to meta import in the above example, even in the case where public meta import is necessary. (Or at least, deemed necessary by the checks. For all I know hypothetically the checks could be wrong, as I'm not exactly sure how lean ferries IR around!)

If you're comfortable opening a zip: shake-test.zip

Or, if you want the modules:

code

ShakeTest.Source

module

public def baz : Bool := true

ShakeTest.Use

module

public meta import ShakeTest.Source

meta def foo : Bool := baz

public meta def bar : Bool := foo

lake build && lake shake --fix && lake build fails there. The issue seems to be laundering the reference through a private meta def.
Is this the same as lean#14427? (mentioned earlier at #mathlib4 > shake)
Yep that one is on my short-term todo list. Also medium-term we should be able to get rid of this specific @[inline] restriction

By the way, as another edge case: I noticed that meta constants can be used in non-meta types and vice-versa without erroring directly, since checkMeta only ever checks the IR value in which they've been erased.

It seems fairly unlikely to me that you would be able to actually get non-sorried code in which shake produced an incorrect recommendation due to this in practice (usually importing what you need to construct an element of that type would also import the type itself at the same phase)...but for the sake of probing the edge case, if Foo is non-meta and imported plainly, we have e.g. meta def x : (fun _ b => b) Foo Bool := true being accepted while shake suggests changing Foo's import to meta import.
